course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Cold War and Decolonization
unit.description: Study how the Cold War divided the world, how colonies won independence, how new states and movements challenged established power, and why the Cold War ended.

stimulusBlocks.attribution: George H. W. Bush, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 31, 1990
stimulusBlocks.citation: George H. W. Bush, Address on the State of the Union, January 31, 1990. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/1990-Bush.txt).
stimulusBlocks.note: Names appear as printed in the transcript, without diacritical marks: Lech Wałęsa led the Polish trade union Solidarity, and Václav Havel was a dissident Czech playwright. Erich Honecker led East Germany until October 1989.
stimulusBlocks.text:
The events of the year just ended, the Revolution of '89, have been a chain reaction, changes so striking that it marks the beginning of a new era in the world's affairs. . . .

A year ago in Poland, Lech Walesa declared that he was ready to open a dialog with the Communist rulers of that country; and today, with the future of a free Poland in their own hands, members of Solidarity lead the Polish Government.

A year ago, freedom's playwright, Vaclav Havel, languished as a prisoner in Prague. And today it's Vaclav Havel, President of Czechoslovakia.

And 1 year ago, Erich Honecker of East Germany claimed history as his guide, and he predicted the Berlin Wall would last another hundred years. And today, less than 1 year later, it's the Wall that's history.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does the passage use as evidence of change?
choices: Havel's move from prisoner to president
The building of the Berlin Wall
The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
Honecker's continued rule in 1990
questions.explanation: Havel's rise shows how quickly power changed hands.
choiceExplanations: Havel's rise shows how quickly power changed hands.
The Wall had fallen.
The passage does not mention Afghanistan.
Honecker's prediction failed.
questions.distinguisher: Honecker appears in the passage, but as a ruler whose prediction failed.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.8 key concept: Soviet economic weakness, costly military commitments, and Gorbachev's reforms led to the end of the Cold War
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the end of the Cold War, 1979–1991
stimulusBlocks.text:
By the 1980s, the Soviet economy was stagnating. The war in Afghanistan drained money and morale, falling oil prices cut export earnings, and a US military buildup under President Ronald Reagan raised the cost of competing.

Mikhail Gorbachev, who took power in 1985, introduced glasnost, or openness, and perestroika, the restructuring of the economy. When Eastern Europeans rose up in 1989, he refused to send troops. The reforms weakened central control, and in December 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved into fifteen independent states.

questions.distinguisher: Stagnation was a cause, but an internal one.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 8.8 key concept: reforms in the Soviet Union and revolutions in Eastern Europe ended the Cold War
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Soviet reform and collapse, 1985–1991
stimulusBlocks.text:
When Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985, the economy was stagnating and the war in Afghanistan, begun in 1979, was costly. He introduced perestroika, a restructuring of the economy that allowed limited private enterprise, and glasnost, a policy of openness that loosened censorship. Glasnost allowed citizens and the press to criticize the government and the Communist Party.

In 1989 Gorbachev refused to send Soviet troops to prevent Eastern European communist governments from falling, and by the end of 1991 the Soviet Union had dissolved into fifteen independent states.

questions.prompt: Glasnost contributed to the collapse of the Soviet Union primarily by
choices: restoring strict censorship in the Soviet republics
ending the war in Afghanistan and withdrawing troops
restoring private ownership of all Soviet industry
allowing criticism of the party and encouraging nationalism
questions.explanation: Openness let citizens criticize the party, and nationalist movements in republics such as the Baltic states gained strength.
choiceExplanations: Glasnost loosened censorship.
The war in Afghanistan ended in 1989, but glasnost was a policy of openness.
Perestroika allowed limited private enterprise, and not all industry.
Openness let citizens criticize the party, and nationalist movements in republics such as the Baltic states gained strength.
questions.distinguisher: Ending the Afghan war eased a burden, but it did not weaken the party's control in the way open criticism did.
